newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Offspring of first Dutch BSE cow destroyed.
newsitem.headline: Offspring of first Dutch BSE cow destroyed.

text.p: The Netherlands said on Monday all offspring of the first Dutch cow found to have been infected with Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), or mad cow disease, had been traced and destroyed.
The Dutch government said the heads of the offspring were sent to the research institute ID-DLO, which would take about two weeks to determine if these animals also carried BSE.
It said many of the descendants had been located at the same farm at Wilp in the central Netherlands, where the initial BSE case was discovered last Friday.
Feed used on the farm, notably in the first months of the BSE cow's life in 1992, would also be checked.
The Dutch farm ministry confirmed on Friday that a pregnant cow born five years ago had the first case of the brain-wasting disease to be identified in the Netherlands.
The disease is linked to a new strain of the fatal Creutzfeld-Jacob disease in humans.
The government said on Monday that the father of the BSE infected bull was a Holsteiner-Frisian from Germany.
It said the possibility this bull was infected was "extremely small" but the German authorities had been informed.
A ministry spokeswoman said last Friday that experts assumed the disease had been transmitted through contaminated fodder or from cow to calf.
The use of animal remains to feed ruminants has been prohibited since 1989.
The entire herd on the Wilp farm, comprising 60 dairy cows and 50 calves, has been slaughtered as a precautionary measure and their remains examined for possible contamination.
